ROLE: You are the Lead Litematica DSL Architect. Your mission is to compile architectural plans into syntactically perfect Litematica DSL code that matches the Java Parser specification.

COORDINATE SYSTEM:
- X: Width, Y: Height (Start at 0), Z: Depth.

TECHNICAL SPECIFICATION:
1. PALETTE: 'palette' ... 'end_palette'. Map 1-char keys to block IDs: 'A = minecraft:stone'. '.' is air.
2. GRID LAYERS: 'layer_y Y OffsetX OffsetZ'. Every subsequent line is a row of Z-depth. End with 'end_layer'.
3. COMMANDS: 'set X Y Z BLOCK', 'fill X1 Y1 Z1 X2 Y2 Z2 BLOCK', 'box', 'carve'.

CONSTRAINTS: No conversational filler. Output raw code only.

Architect's Plan:
Listen closely, Student. Before we place a single block, we must see the structure in our mind's eye. We are building a 2D pixel art representation of a Minion. I will guide you through the spatial rationale so you can bridge the gap between raw coordinates and architectural intent.

1. Footprint Analysis
I will establish a bounding box with the dimensions X=2 (Depth), Z=12 (Width), and Y=19 (Height). This is not a fully 3D hollow or solid building; it is a vertical, solid pixel art canvas. The structure is primarily flat—exactly 1 block thick along the X=0 axis. However, I will make the very bottom layer (Y=0) 2 blocks deep (X=0 and X=1) to create a tiered, extruded base. This gives the flat artwork a stable physical stand so it does not look paper-thin where it meets the ground.

2. Material Strategy
I will use a highly restricted, stylized palette to bring this pixel art to life:
- White Wool (B): This is my primary canvas. I will use it for the Minion's body, overalls, and the whites of its eyes. Wool provides a clean, matte texture that is perfect for flat pixel art.
- Stone (C): I will use Stone exclusively for the Minion's goggles. The grey, solid, slightly rugged texture of stone perfectly mimics the thick metallic frames of the goggles, creating a visual contrast against the soft wool.
- Oak Leaves (A): I will use these only at the bottom corners of the build. They act as small decorative bushes or ground anchors, framing the piece and giving it a connection to the earth.

3. Construction Sequence
I will build this from the ground up, layer by layer, keeping the 2D profile in mind.

At Y=0, I will lay down the foundation and the stand. I will place Oak Leaves at the far left (Z=0) and far right (Z=11) edges. In the center (Z=4 and Z=7), I will place White Wool for the Minion's feet. I will extend this entire layer to be 2 blocks deep (X=0 and X=1) to ensure the structure has a sturdy base.

At Y=1, I will transition to a strictly 1-block depth (X=0) for the rest of the build. I will build the ankles using White Wool directly above the feet.

At Y=2 and Y=3, I will begin forming the lower body and overalls. I will expand the White Wool outward, growing the width from 4 blocks to 6 blocks to create the curved bottom of the Minion.

From Y=4 to Y=11, I will construct the main cylindrical torso. I will rapidly expand the width to 8 blocks, then 10 blocks, until I hit the maximum width of 12 blocks between Y=6 and Y=9. This forms the fat, pill-like shape of the character. At Y=10 and Y=11, I will slightly taper the sides back to 10 blocks wide to define the upper head area.

From Y=12 to Y=15, I will construct the focal point of the art: the goggles and eyes. 
- At Y=12, I will lay a horizontal line of Stone to form the thick lower rim of the goggles, flanked by White Wool for the sides of the head.
- At Y=13 and Y=14, I will build the lenses. I will use Stone for the outer frames and the center bridge. I will fill the negative space inside these frames with White Wool to represent the large, wide-open eyes.
- At Y=15, I will cap the goggles with another horizontal line of Stone for the upper rim.

At Y=16 and Y=17, I will build the top of the head. I will use White Wool and aggressively taper the width down to 8 blocks, and finally to 4 blocks at the very top. This creates the smooth, iconic dome shape of the Minion's head.

At Y=18, I will leave the layer completely empty (Air). This acts as the spatial ceiling of our bounding box, confirming the structure is complete. 

By following this logic, I ensure that every coordinate serves a visual purpose, turning a grid of letters into a recognizable, standing piece of art.

Architect's Plan:
As your Master Teacher, I will guide you through the spatial visualization of the "Cool Nether Portal." We are going to construct a dark, gothic, and corrupted gateway. 

1. Footprint Analysis
I am working with a footprint that is 11 blocks along the X-axis, 13 blocks along the Z-axis, and stretches 17 blocks high on the Y-axis. The structure is tiered and features a hollow center where the portal itself resides. The portal frame is oriented along the Z-axis, meaning a traveler will walk through it facing down the X-axis. The main architectural mass occupies the first 5 blocks of the X-axis (X=0 to X=4), while the remaining space (X=5 to X=10) is dedicated to a sprawling, corrupted ground layer that bleeds outward from the gateway.

2. Material Strategy
I will use a heavily textured palette of Blackstone variants (polished, cracked, chiseled, and bricks) to give the structure a ruined, ancient, and oppressive gothic weight. For the functional gateway, I must use Obsidian. To create a menacing, fiery aesthetic, I will use Magma blocks encased in Dark Iron Bars—this will look like hellfire trapped within cages. To blend the portal into the Overworld, I will use Soul Sand, Soul Soil, Coarse Dirt, and Gravel to simulate a creeping "Nether infection" corrupting the surrounding Grass and Dirt. Finally, Wither Skeleton Skulls will serve as macabre gargoyles.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic

At Y=0, I am laying the corrupted foundation. I will place standard grass and dirt around the outer edges, but directly beneath and in front of the portal (stretching out to X=10), I will aggressively mix soul sand, soul soil, gravel, and coarse dirt. I am doing this to visually tell the story that the Nether's dark magic is leaking into the Overworld and killing the earth.

At Y=1, I am building the structural base. I will place a 5-block line of Obsidian along the Z-axis (Z=4 to Z=8) at X=2 to form the bottom of the portal frame. Flanking this frame on both sides (Z=1 to Z=3, and Z=9 to Z=11), I will construct thick, 3x3 pedestals using solid blackstone. I will ring these pedestals with blackstone stairs to slope the foundation upward, giving it a heavy, anchored feel.

From Y=2 to Y=9, I am raising the portal sides and the flanking pillars. I will build the Obsidian portal frame up to a height of 8 blocks on the Z=3 and Z=9 lines. On the pedestals beside the frame, I will construct two massive pillars. To make them glow with inner heat, I will build a central core of Magma blocks and wrap them in Dark Iron Bars. I will frame these iron cages with a randomized mix of polished, cracked, and chiseled blackstone blocks. On the outer edges of these pillars, I will attach blackstone walls and buttons to add jagged, gothic greebling.

At Y=10, I am closing the portal lintel and capping the pillars. I will place Obsidian across the top to connect the two sides of the frame. Above the caged magma pillars, I will use inverted stairs and solid blackstone to seal the iron bars, visually containing the fire within the columns.

At Y=11 and Y=12, I am starting the roof and the glowing crown. I will place a secondary layer of Magma blocks directly above the portal lintel and the pillar caps to create a fiery crest. I will then use blackstone slabs and stairs to taper the roofline inwards, creating a heavy, sloped archway that shields the portal.

From Y=13 to Y=16, I am constructing the final spires. I will build tall, jagged spikes on top of the two flanking pillars using a mix of blackstone walls and magma blocks, tapering them sharply until they end at a single block at Y=16. To complete the sinister aesthetic, I will mount Wither Skeleton Skulls onto the sides of these spires and above the central arch. These skulls will act as dark guardians, staring down at anyone foolish enough to approach the gateway.

Architect's Plan:
Footprint Analysis:
I will build a structure that is 17 blocks wide (X), 9 blocks deep (Z), and 7 blocks tall (Y). This building is a hollow, box-like factory with a dense, tiered internal structure designed to house automated brewing machinery. The outer shell is a clean rectangle, while the inside is packed with functional, multi-level components.

Material Strategy:
I will use Quartz Blocks as the primary building material for the exterior shell and structural framework. This gives the factory a clean, modern, and sterile look—perfect for a laboratory or potion facility. I will use Stone heavily in the interior to represent the dense machinery, redstone circuits, and structural supports of the automated system. Dirt and Grass Blocks will be used sparingly at the very bottom to ground the foundation into the earth. I will place Chests for input/output storage, a Crafting Table for manual ingredient preparation, Stone Slabs for half-step machinery alignments, and Torches to ensure the factory is well-lit and safe from mob spawns.

Construction Sequence:
At Y=0, I will lay down the foundation. I will use a mix of Dirt and Quartz to establish the 17x9 footprint. I will place Quartz heavily along the edges and interior supports, embedding a few Stone blocks for structural anchors and a Grass block at the front edge to blend the factory with the outside terrain.

At Y=1, I will build the ground floor and the base of the machinery. I will construct a solid Quartz perimeter to enclose the factory. Inside, I will leave open air spaces for walkways, but I will lay down intricate Stone and Quartz patterns to form the base of the automated brewing system. I will place a Chest at the front left to serve as the primary output collection point for finished potions.

At Y=2, I will continue raising the outer walls with Quartz. Inside, I will build the second tier of the machinery using dense Stone blocks. I will place a Crafting Table near the front output chest for quick access to ingredient crafting, and I will add a Stone Slab and Torches to begin detailing the internal mechanisms and providing necessary light.

At Y=3, I will build the middle tier of the factory. I will maintain the Quartz outer shell. Inside, I will construct the central brewing columns using Stone. I will place several Torches along the inner Quartz walls and machinery to ensure the complex internal layout is brightly illuminated and easy to inspect.

At Y=4, I will construct the upper-middle section. I will place a distinct alternating pattern of Torches along the back inner wall to create a bright, functional display area, which serves to monitor the status of the brewing process. I will continue routing the Stone machinery blocks through the center, connecting the lower outputs to the upper inputs.

At Y=5, I will build the top layer of the machinery. I will place additional Chests on the left side to act as the bulk input storage for water bottles and raw ingredients. I will cap off the internal Stone mechanisms, ensuring everything is positioned to feed downward into the systems I built in the lower layers.

At Y=6, I will construct the roof. I will cover almost the entire 17x9 area with a solid layer of Quartz Blocks to seal the factory and protect the delicate machinery inside. I will leave a small air gap on the left side to serve as a maintenance hatch or ventilation shaft for the brewing fumes.

Architect's Plan:
I am designing a structure called Large Presents. I will create a footprint that spans 8 blocks on the X-axis, 5 blocks on the Z-axis, and reaches 7 blocks high on the Y-axis. The structure consists of two distinct boxes: a large 5x5x5 primary present and a smaller 3x3x3 secondary present nestled directly beside it. I will make the interiors hollow to save materials, as these are decorative structures, but the outer shells will be solid to maintain the illusion of heavy, wrapped boxes.

I must choose materials that mimic vibrant wrapping paper and shiny ribbons. For the large present, I will use Red Concrete for the wrapping paper because its smooth, saturated texture gives a clean, festive look without the visual noise of traditional stone or wood. For its ribbon, I will use Yellow Wool to provide a soft, matte contrast to the concrete. For the smaller present, I will use Green Concrete for the wrapping and White Quartz Block for the ribbon, creating a crisp, bright accent. I will also use Yellow Wool and Quartz Stairs at the very top for the bows to add depth and realistic folds to the ribbons.

I will build this layer by layer to ensure the ribbons align perfectly across the 3D space.

At Y=0, I am laying the foundation. I will build a 5x5 square outline of Red Concrete from X=0 to X=4, and Z=0 to Z=4. I will leave the center 3x3 hollow. Next to it, from X=5 to X=7, and Z=2 to Z=4, I will lay a 3x3 square outline of Green Concrete for the smaller present. I will replace the exact middle block of each wall with my ribbon materials to start the vertical wrap: Yellow Wool at the center of the red walls, and White Quartz at the center of the green walls.

At Y=1, I will extrude the walls upward exactly as they are in Y=0. The hollow interiors remain empty. The ribbons on the sides of both presents will continue straight up the center of each face, dividing the concrete into neat quadrants.

At Y=2, I am capping off the smaller green present while continuing the walls of the red one. For the green present, I will fill its roof with Green Concrete, crossing the center with White Quartz to complete its ribbon over the top. The red present simply gets another layer of its hollow wall pattern.

At Y=3, I am adding the bow to the smaller present and continuing the large present. I will place two White Quartz Stairs facing each other on top of the green present's center to act as a small, pinched bow. For the large present, I will continue building the hollow Red Concrete walls with the Yellow Wool ribbon in the center of each face.

I will use Oak Planks (F) at the transition layer to provide a warm, residential floor for the upstairs apartment.
I will use Quartz Blocks (G) for the interior walls of the second floor, giving the laboratory a clean, slightly sterile contrast to the brick exterior.
I will use a Furnace (H) and Bookshelves (I) to represent the chaotic lab equipment—most notably, the microwave (PhoneWave) and research clutter.

I will use Iron Blocks for the primary conductive pathways where redstone signals must travel, giving the module a clean, industrial, and engineered aesthetic. I will use Stone for the structural anchor points and capping blocks. This creates a visual and logical distinction between the active circuitry lines and the inert physical supports.

I will now walk through the construction sequence layer by layer. 

At Y=0, I will establish the base of the module. I will place a single Iron Block at X=3. This serves as the foundational pillar that will eventually support a redstone torch to lock the sorting hoppers above.

At Y=1, I will build directly upward. I will place another Iron Block at X=3, extending the central pillar and leaving the rest of the layer completely empty to allow space for adjacent redstone components.

At Y=2, I will expand the structure horizontally to create the lower component shelf. I will place an alternating line of blocks starting from X=1 to X=4. I will place Stone at X=1 and X=3 to act as structural mounts, and I will place Iron Blocks at X=2 and X=4 to serve as conductive platforms for a repeater and redstone dust.

I will use Stone as my primary building block for the base and the redstone platforms because it is a solid, opaque block that reliably transmits redstone power. I will use Glass to enclose the growing chamber; this is crucial because I want to visually monitor the farm's operation, and glass is a transparent block that will not inadvertently conduct redstone signals and cause short circuits. I will use Sand as the specific substrate required to plant the kelp. For the automation, I will use an Observer, Piston, and Dispenser to create a rapid-growth and harvesting loop. Finally, I will use a vertical chain of Chests, Hoppers, and a Furnace to create a gravity-fed logistics system that automatically cooks the raw kelp into dried kelp. I will attach Ladders to the stone spine to ensure I can climb up to inspect the system and access the storage.

Construction Sequence:
At Y=0, I will begin by placing a double chest at the very bottom. This is my final output destination where the finished Dried Kelp will accumulate. 

At Y=1, I will place a hopper pointing directly down into that output chest. 

At Y=2, I will place a furnace directly on top of that hopper. This furnace is the heart of the "drying" process. Next to it, I will place another hopper feeding into the side of the furnace for fuel. In the back corner, I will lay the first stone blocks of my structural spine and attach a ladder to begin my vertical accessway.

At Y=3, I will build the intermediate storage. I will place a double chest and a hopper to feed raw kelp down into the top of the furnace. I will place an oak wall sign to label this chest. In the back, I will expand the stone platform and lay down redstone wire and a redstone wall torch. This is the beginning of the clock circuit that will power the farm.

At Y=4, I will place the most important block of the farm: the Sand block. This is the floor of the growth chamber. Behind the sand, I will place a repeater and more redstone dust on the stone platform, along with a lever. I will use this lever as a master switch to turn the farm's automated clock on and off. I will also add another chest and hopper for bonemeal input, labeling it with a sign.

At Y=5, I will plant the Kelp directly onto the sand. Right next to the kelp, I will place a dispenser facing inward; this will shoot bonemeal to force the kelp to grow instantly. I will surround this entire layer with glass to contain the water block that the kelp requires to survive. 

At Y=6, I will install the harvesting mechanism. I will place a piston facing the space directly above the base kelp stalk. When the redstone wire behind it fires, the piston will extend and snap the kelp. I will continue building the glass enclosure to hold the water. I will also place the primary collection chest and hoppers here to catch the broken kelp as it floats to the top of the water.

At Y=7, I will place an observer block facing the water column, directly above the piston. I am placing it here so that the moment the kelp grows into this space, the observer will detect the block update and send a redstone pulse down the back wall to trigger the piston below it. I will surround the rest of this layer with glass to keep the water contained.

At Y=8, I will finish the build by placing a solid glass roof directly over the water column. I must do this to cap the chamber; otherwise, the broken kelp items might shoot out of the top of the farm instead of flowing sideways into my collection hoppers.

1. Footprint Analysis
I will define the bounding box of this structure. The X-axis (width) is 9 blocks. The Y-axis (height) is 13 blocks, running from Y=0 to Y=12. The Z-axis (depth) is 17 blocks. 
This is not a solid building; it is a highly specialized, encased redstone machine. It is structurally tiered and mostly hollow on the inside to accommodate complex circuitry. The front face (Z=1) is a flat, solid display screen, while the main body (Z=2 through Z=16) houses the counting logic, protected by transparent outer walls.

2. Material Strategy
I will use specific materials to separate structural integrity from mechanical logic:
- Stone (A): I will use this as my primary structural frame, the unlit segments of the display screen, and the solid conductive blocks required for redstone repeaters and torches.
- White Wool (B): I will use this as my dedicated wiring block. Using wool allows me to visually trace the counting logic and separate the circuitry from the structural frame.
- Bedrock (C): I will use this exclusively on the front display face (Z=1). It provides an unbreakable, high-contrast, dark background to make the 7-segment display pop.
- Glass (D): I will use this to build the side walls and the roof. This encases the machine while allowing observers to see the internal counting mechanics. Crucially, I will also use Glass internally within the circuitry; because it is a transparent, non-conductive block, it prevents adjacent redstone lines from short-circuiting.
- Stone Slab (E): I will use these half-blocks to transmit redstone signals steeply upward without cutting off the wire, which a full solid block would do.

3. Construction Sequence
I will build this machine layer by layer, ensuring the logic flows upward from the input to the display.

Layer Y=0 (The Foundation): I will lay down the base footprint. I will build a solid Stone line at Z=1 to serve as the foundation for the display screen, and another solid Stone line at the back (Z=16). On the left side, I will place a few Wool and Stone blocks to establish the initial input signal pathway.

Layer Y=1 (Display Base & Lower Logic): I will begin the display face at Z=1, using Bedrock for the background and Stone for the bottom border. I will establish the Glass side walls to start enclosing the machine. Inside, I will lay out the first horizontal Wool wiring lines to distribute the incoming signal toward the lower display segments.

Layer Y=2 (Bottom Horizontal Segment): At the front display face, I will place three Stone blocks flanked by Bedrock to form the bottom horizontal segment of the '8'. Internally, I will step the Wool wiring up diagonally and introduce the first Stone Slabs near the back to carry signals upward efficiently.

Layers Y=3 to Y=5 (Lower Vertical Segments & Mid-Logic): I will build the lower vertical segments of the display using Stone blocks separated by Bedrock. Inside the machine, the logic becomes dense. I will construct a complex matrix of Wool and Stone. At Y=4 and Y=5, I will strategically place internal Glass blocks to isolate adjacent redstone lines, ensuring the counting mechanism remains accurate and does not cross-wire.

Layer Y=6 (Middle Horizontal Segment): I will form the middle horizontal segment on the display face. Inside, I will build a dense Stone platform across the center. This acts as a physical and conductive divider between the lower counting circuits and the upper counting circuits.

Layers Y=7 to Y=9 (Upper Vertical Segments & Upper Logic): I will construct the upper vertical segments on the front face. Internally, the wiring becomes sparser as signals reach their destinations. I will use Wool to route the final signals to the top segments, and I will use a line of Stone Slabs at Y=9 to step the redstone lines smoothly toward the very top of the display.

Layer Y=10 (Top Horizontal Segment): I will place the final three Stone blocks on the display face to complete the top horizontal segment of the '8'. Inside, I will mirror the slab placements with solid Stone to finalize the circuit connections to the screen.

Layer Y=11 (The Crown): I will cap the display face with a solid horizontal line of Bedrock. The interior cavity is now completely empty (Air) because all logic lines have successfully connected to the display face below. The Glass walls continue to enclose the empty space.

Layer Y=12 (The Roof): I will seal the machine. I will place solid Stone at the front and back edges for structural framing, and I will fill the entire center of the roof with Glass. This acts as a skylight, illuminating the counter's internal logic while keeping the redstone safe from the elements.

- Stone Slab (C): I will use these sparingly to create a sleek counter or card-return ledge for the player interface.
- Chest (D): I will place these at the very top to act as the functional input/output of the game—this is where the player will receive their cards or winnings.

At Y=0 and Y=1, I will lay down two identical, completely solid 12x12 layers of Stone. This creates a massive, unmovable foundation for the machine, ensuring the delicate mechanics above are fully supported.

At Y=2, I will begin raising the ground floor walls. I will outline the 10x11 footprint with Quartz, but I will intentionally leave large gaps in the walls. Welcome, student. Today we are analyzing the "Safe fully equiped starter house". The name itself dictates our architectural priorities: absolute security from hostile mobs, high survival utility, and efficient use of early-game resources. 

1. Footprint Analysis
I will build this structure within a 15x14 footprint (X=0 to 14, Z=0 to 13) and raise it to a height of 8 blocks (Y=0 to 7). The architecture is a hollow, functional living space attached to a secure front yard, topped with a tiered, flat, mob-proof roof. 

2. Material Strategy
I must choose materials that balance safety with accessibility. 
- I will use Cobblestone extensively for the floor and roof parapets because it provides excellent blast resistance against Creepers. 
- I will use Oak Logs to frame the corners, giving the structure visual weight and structural logic. 
- I will use Oak Planks for the walls to provide a warm, traditional domestic feel. 
- I will use Stone for pathways, yard boundaries, and roof reinforcements to create clean, durable accents.
- I will integrate an indoor Water source, Chests, a Crafting Table, and a massive bank of Furnaces to fulfill the "fully equipped" promise.
- I will use an overwhelming number of Torches. A "safe" house must have zero dark spots to prevent mob spawns.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic
Let us walk through the layers so you can visualize the construction process.

Layer Y=0 (The Foundation): 
I will prepare the ground by laying a 15x14 bed of Dirt and Grass to seamlessly integrate the house into the natural terrain. At the coordinates X=2-3 and Z=7-8, I will place a small cluster of Cobblestone. I am doing this to line the bottom of an indoor well, ensuring the water does not leak into the dirt.

Layer Y=1 (The Floor & Infinite Water): 
I will lay down a solid 12x12 Cobblestone floor to ensure nothing can dig up from below, and explosions won't easily destroy the foundation. Directly over the well foundation I built in Y=0, I will place Water blocks to create a 2x2 infinite water source right inside the house. I will also lay a Stone pathway at the front (Z=13) to guide the player to the entrance.

Layer Y=2 (First Walls & Utility Placement): 
I will establish the main living box (spanning Z=1 to 9). I will place Oak Logs at the corners for strong pillars, and fill the gaps with Oak Planks and Stone. Because this is a "fully equipped" base, I will immediately populate the interior: I will place Chests for storage, a Crafting Table for immediate use, and begin a bank of Furnaces on the right wall. Outside the main door (Z=10 to 12), I will outline a secure front yard using Stone blocks.

Layer Y=3 & Y=4 (Upper Walls & Illumination): 
I will continue raising the walls, maintaining the Oak Log pillars and Plank siding. I will stack more Furnaces on top of the ones from Layer 2, creating a highly efficient, industrial-scale smelting wall. To guarantee the "safe" aspect of this build, I will aggressively place Torches on the interior walls, the exterior walls, and around the front yard. I should leave no shadow untouched.

Layer Y=5 (The Fortified Ceiling): 
I will cap the living space with a heavy-duty ceiling. I will build a thick outer ring of Stone and fill the center with Cobblestone and Oak Planks. This solid, blast-resistant layer protects the player from lightning strikes and falling mobs. 

Layer Y=6 (The Roof Parapet): 
Instead of a sloped roof, I will build a hollow Cobblestone ring around the perimeter of the roof. This acts as a parapet—a low protective wall. I am building this so the player can safely climb onto the roof and shoot arrows at surrounding monsters without the risk of being knocked off.

Layer Y=7 (The Crown of Light): 
Finally, I will place a continuous ring of Torches directly on top of the Layer 6 Cobblestone parapet. I will do this to ensure the roof is entirely spawn-proof. A flat roof is dangerous if unlit, but this crown of fire guarantees our starter house remains a true safe haven.

I will use Gravel as a gravity-affected block, acting as a physical update trigger or a temporary weight in this mechanical abstraction. 
I will use Glass to create transparent side-walls in the mechanical layer, allowing visibility into the inner workings while preventing redstone signal crossing. 
Finally, I will use Furnaces as immovable utility blocks. In mechanical doors, I must use these to prevent adjacent moving parts (like slime blocks) from pulling the surrounding walls apart.

I will lay down a 3x6 base. I will construct this mostly out of Quartz to give the mechanism a clean, flat floor, but I will embed two Stone blocks along the central axis. I will use these Stone blocks to mark the heavy anchor points for the mechanism above.

I will use Oak Planks to accent the corners of this stone base, visually tying the masonry to the woodwork above. I will be working within a bounding box of X=9 (0 to 8), Y=12 (0 to 11), and Z=7 (0 to 6). This structure is highly tiered and functional. It is not a solid building, nor is it a hollow room. It is a mechanical skeleton. The lower half (Y=0 to Y=5) represents the subterranean redstone trench. Y=6 is the actual ground level where the player walks. The upper half (Y=7 to Y=11) forms the door frame and the overhead circuitry housing. 

2. Material Strategy
I will use exactly one material for this entire build: Stone (minecraft:stone). Why? Because this is a redstone blueprint. I need a solid, opaque block that reliably conducts redstone power. Stone does not burn, it cannot be moved by Endermen, and it provides a clean, neutral background that makes debugging redstone dust, repeaters, and torches visually easier. It is the perfect structural anchor for heavy piston machinery.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic
I will build this layer by layer, starting from the deepest part of the underground circuit.

At Y=0 and Y=1, I will lay the foundational wiring trenches. I will create a long central line across the X-axis at Z=3. This Z=3 line is the absolute center axis of the door. I will also build a perpendicular spur at X=4 (Z=1 to Z=5). This cross-shape ensures the redstone signal can reach the very bottom-center pistons that will push the floor blocks upward.

At Y=2 and Y=3, I will begin raising the vertical support columns. I will place blocks at the far edges (X=0 and X=8) along the Z=3 axis, and build a solid line across the back at Z=6. These act as the vertical signal towers, carrying the redstone power from the underground trench up to the surface.

At Y=4 and Y=5, I am just below the surface. I will build a wide sub-floor platform in the front (X=2 to 6, Z=1 and 2). This platform will support the intricate wiring needed for the double-piston extenders that are characteristic of large, improved redstone doors. I will also fill in the central door threshold at Z=3.

At Y=6, I will construct the main walking floor. This is a massive, nearly solid layer spanning almost the entire 9x7 footprint. This is the "ground zero" for the player. Everything built before this layer is hidden underground. 

At Y=7, Y=8, and Y=9, I will erect the upper door frame and the side pillars. I will build strong vertical columns at X=1 and X=7. I am intentionally leaving the center (X=2 to X=6) completely hollow. This negative space is the actual doorway the player will walk through. The pillars at X=1 and X=7 will hide the side-pushing pistons and continue carrying the redstone signal up to the roof. I will also maintain a solid line of stone at Z=3 to act as the lintel of the door.

At Y=10, I will place the ceiling layer. I will build a solid central mass from X=2 to 6. This caps the hallway, enclosing the mechanical space and providing a flat base for the final layer of circuitry.

Finally, at Y=11, I will finish with the top wiring ring. I will build a hollow rectangular frame (X=2 to 6, Z=0 to 6) with a single, crucial central node at X=4, Z=3. This top ring will house the redstone dust that powers the top-down pistons, completing the circuit and allowing the door to close seamlessly from all four sides.

I will design this structure within a footprint that is 10 blocks wide on the X-axis, 8 blocks deep on the Z-axis, and 6 blocks tall on the Y-axis. The structure will transition from a solid foundation to a hollow, functional workspace, topped with a tiered, fireproof roof.

My material strategy is dictated by the building's purpose. I will use Cobblestone heavily on the right side of the build; this is the forge area, and I need a fire-resistant material to contain the extreme heat. I will use Oak Planks for the floor on the left side to provide a comfortable, dry living and working space for the hunter. I will frame the walls with Oak Logs for structural strength and a rugged aesthetic. I will use smooth Stone for work surfaces, anvils, and structural accents. Lava will serve as the raw, beating heart of the forge, while Furnaces will be used for practical smelting. Finally, I will use Stone Slabs to cap the roof, giving it a clean, fortified trim.

Let us walk through the construction sequence, layer by layer.

At Y=0, I will lay the foundation. I must establish the divide between the two zones immediately. On the right side, I will pour a thick, solid bed of cobblestone to support the heavy forge. On the left, I will lay a neat floor of oak planks. Near the front edge, I will place a small cluster of stone blocks just outside the main footprint to serve as an exterior step or outdoor grinding stone.

At Y=1, I will begin raising the walls and installing the utilities. On the right side, I will build a thick cobblestone enclosure and carefully place two blocks of raw lava inside it. This is the forge's heat source. I will place a chest right next to it so I can quickly store smelted ingots or raw meat. On the left side, I will erect thick oak log pillars to frame the hunter's room, placing a few stone blocks around the floor to act as low workbenches or anvils. 

At Y=2, I will continue building the walls upward. I will mix oak logs and stone blocks on the left side to create a sturdy, textured wall, leaving intentional air gaps that will serve as unglazed windows to let out smoke and let in light. On the right side, above the lava pit, I will place a furnace. I am positioning it here so it conceptually draws heat directly from the lava below. 

At Y=3, I will bring the walls to their maximum height. I will solidify the oak log framing on the left. On the right, I will continue building up the cobblestone to act as a massive chimney, and I will place a second furnace adjacent to the first to maximize my smelting capacity. 

At Y=4, I will construct the primary roof. Because this building houses open lava and active furnaces, a wooden roof would be a fatal mistake. Therefore, I will lay a completely solid, flat ceiling of cobblestone across the entire 10x7 interior footprint. This seals the room, traps the heat where it belongs, and ensures the building will not catch fire.

At Y=5, I will add the final architectural polish. A flat cobblestone roof is functional but ugly. I will place a continuous ring of stone slabs around the absolute perimeter of the roof. I will leave the center of this layer hollow. This creates a tiered, parapet effect that gives the HunterForge a fortified, professional silhouette while saving on building materials.

I am building a classic, 5-slice 'Item Sorter' (often known as the ImpulseSV design). Before I place a single block, I must understand the footprint. The structure is 11 blocks wide (X=0 to 10), 6 blocks tall (Y=0 to 5), and 11 blocks deep (Z=0 to 10). It is a tiered, highly functional redstone build. It is mostly hollow where the player stands, but incredibly dense with storage and logic components in the active slices from Z=2 to Z=6. 

For my material strategy, I will use Quartz Blocks as my primary structural and conductive material. Quartz has a clean texture, making it easy to debug redstone lines. I will use Chests for bulk storage and Hoppers to transport and filter the items. To build the logic brain of the sorter, I will use Redstone Comparators to measure item volume, Redstone Wire (dust) to transmit signals, Repeaters to boost and direct power, and Redstone Wall Torches to act as the locking mechanism for the hoppers.

I will construct this layer by layer, focusing on how the 3D space creates a cascading redstone circuit:

At Y=0, I will place a single Quartz block at the origin (0,0,0). This acts as a foundational alignment marker for the schematic. The rest of this layer is left as empty air.

At Y=1, I will begin the first tier of the storage system. Working across the active slices from Z=2 to Z=6, I will place double chests at X=3 and X=4. Directly behind them at X=5, I will place hoppers pointing into these chests. At X=8, leaving a two-block gap, I will place a row of Quartz blocks. These blocks are crucial; they will serve as the floor to support the repeaters in the next layer.

At Y=2, I will build the second tier of storage and begin the locking mechanism. I will place another set of double chests at X=3 and X=4, with hoppers at X=5 feeding into them. Now, I will build the lower redstone logic. I will place Quartz blocks at X=7 and X=9. In the gap between them at X=8, I will place Repeaters facing the blocks at X=7. On the side of the X=7 Quartz blocks (occupying the X=6 space), I will attach Redstone Wall Torches. These torches sit directly under the hoppers of the next layer, keeping them locked by default so items don't flow through uncontrollably.

Architect's Plan:
Welcome, Student. Today we are studying a masterpiece of technical Minecraft architecture: ilmango's Melon & Pumpkin Farm. Before you look at a single line of code, I want you to close your eyes and visualize the machine we are about to build. 

1. Footprint Analysis
The total bounding box of this structure is 13 blocks wide (X), 16 blocks deep (Z), and 9 blocks tall (Y). However, the core functional footprint is a perfectly dense 9x9 square. This is not a hollow building; it is a highly tiered, solid-state machine. Every single layer is stacked directly on top of the previous one with zero wasted space, forming a compact, self-contained agricultural engine.

2. Material Strategy
I will use Stone for the lower foundation because it is a solid, conductive block perfect for supporting rails and transmitting redstone power. 
For the enclosure, I will use White Stained Glass. This creates a physical barrier to prevent harvested items from flying out of the farm, while allowing us to see the machine working and preventing hostile mobs from spawning on the rim.
For the soil, I will use a precise mix of Farmland and Dirt. Stems require Farmland, but the fruit needs a solid Dirt block to spawn on. 
I will use a Shroomlight in the center of the farm. Crops need light to grow, and placing a permanent light source ensures the farm operates at maximum efficiency day or night, even with a roof over it.
Finally, I will use Note Blocks in the redstone wiring. Note blocks are cheap, solid, and instantly update adjacent blocks when powered, making them the perfect trigger for our pistons.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic
Let us walk through the vertical construction, layer by layer.

At Y=0, I will leave the space empty. This is simply a clearance buffer for the schematic.

At Y=1, I will place a row of levers. Their sole purpose is to sit beneath the floor and provide constant, hidden redstone power to the solid blocks above them.

At Y=2, I will build the foundation and the collection hub. I will place a double chest and a hopper at the front. Behind this, I will lay down a 9x11 solid Stone platform. On the edge of this platform, I will build a comparator and redstone torch circuit. This creates an automatic minecart unloader that will stop our collection cart, empty its contents into the chest, and send it back out.

At Y=3, I will lay down the rail network. I will place regular rails and powered rails in a tight zig-zag pattern across the entire 9x9 stone platform. The levers from Y=1 will activate the powered rails. A hopper minecart will run continuously on these tracks, sweeping back and forth to suck up items through the ceiling.

At Y=4, I will construct the farm floor directly above the rails. I will create a 9x9 checkerboard pattern of Farmland and regular Dirt. Right in the dead center of this grid, I will place a single Stone Brick Stair. I will waterlog this stair. A waterlogged stair holds a source block of water to hydrate the entire 9x9 farmland grid, but its solid bottom prevents the water from spilling down and breaking our rails below.

At Y=5, I will plant the crops. I will ring the 9x9 farm area with White Stained Glass to build the walls. Inside, I will plant Pumpkin and Melon stems strictly on the Farmland blocks. I will leave the Dirt blocks empty as air; this is where the fruit will spawn. Directly over the central waterlogged stair, I will place the Shroomlight to bathe the crops in light.

At Y=6, I will install the harvesting mechanics. I will place Observers facing downwards directly over every single stem. Whenever a stem bends to connect to a newly spawned fruit, the Observer will detect it. Over every empty Dirt block, I will place downward-facing Pistons. These are our crushers.

At Y=7, I will wire the brain of the farm. I will place a checkerboard of Note Blocks and Stone directly on top of the Observers and Pistons. When an Observer detects a stem update, it sends a pulse upward into the block above it. This instantly updates the adjacent Note Blocks, which in turn triggers the Pistons to fire downwards, instantly crushing the newly spawned melon or pumpkin. The broken items fall onto the dirt, where the hopper minecart at Y=3 sucks them up.

At Y=8, I will cap the structure. I will place a flat 9x9 roof of Stone Brick Slabs over the redstone. Slabs are unspawnable, protecting our farm from creepers and giving the machine a clean, finished aesthetic.

Visualize this stack, Student: Levers, then Rails, then Soil, then Crops, then Pistons, then Redstone, then Roof. A perfect vertical assembly line. You are now ready to read the coordinates.

Rather than a solid building, this is a hollow, tiered framework. The primary action and mechanical tension occur along the central depth axis (Z=1), while the outer edges (Z=0 and Z=2) serve as the structural boundaries for the elevator shaft. 

Material Strategy:
I will use three specific materials to give this elevator a functional, realistic appearance:
1. Stone: I will use Stone for the heavy, load-bearing mechanical components. It will form the lower motor housing, the upper pulley supports, and the final structural crossbeam at the top.
2. Oak Planks: I will use Oak Planks for the human-facing architecture. This includes the boarding platforms and the long vertical guide rails that form the elevator shaft. It provides a lightweight, scaffold-like contrast to the stone.
3. Obsidian: I will use Obsidian very sparingly—only at the absolute bottom and top of the mechanism. Because it is an immovable block in Minecraft, it perfectly represents the heavy-duty anchors and high-tension winch points required to pull an elevator car.

Construction Sequence:

Base & Lower Motor (Y=0 to Y=2):
I will start by laying the mechanical foundation along the center line (Z=1). At Y=0, I will place a Stone base, an Oak structural block, and an Obsidian anchor at the far right (X=3) to serve as the bottom tension point. Moving up to Y=1 and Y=2, I will build up the Stone motor housing on the right side (X=2 and X=3) and begin the Oak framework on the left. 

Lower Boarding Platform (Y=3):
At Y=3, I will construct the ground-floor boarding area. I will create a U-shape of Oak Planks on the left side (X=0 and X=1) that spans from the front (Z=0) to the back (Z=2). This gives passengers a place to stand. Meanwhile, I will cap the lower Stone machinery on the right side.

Lower Shaft Base (Y=4 to Y=6):
I will now begin the vertical shaft. I will place Oak Planks at Z=0 and Z=2 to act as the front and back guide rails. Between them, I will place a few more Stone blocks to finalize the lower winch system before the shaft becomes completely hollow.

The Vertical Shaft (Y=7 to Y=22):
Here, I will build the main elevator track. For 16 blocks straight up, I will only place Oak Planks at X=1, Z=0 and X=1, Z=2. By leaving the center (Z=1) completely empty, I will create a tall, hollow channel where the elevator car will travel. 

Upper Boarding Platform (Y=23):
At Y=23, I have reached the destination floor. Just like the bottom platform, I will use Oak Planks to create a U-shaped walkway on the left side (X=0 and X=1) spanning the depth of the structure, allowing passengers to safely exit the shaft.

Upper Shaft & Top Pulley (Y=24 to Y=27):
I will continue the Oak guide rails up through Y=24 and Y=25 to ensure the car doesn't derail at the top floor. At Y=26, I will introduce Stone blocks at the far left and right edges (X=0 and X=3) to support the top pulley mechanism. 1. FOOTPRINT ANALYSIS
I am designing a structure that is 16 blocks wide (X), 30 blocks deep (Z), and 6 blocks tall (Y). I must divide this rectangular footprint into two distinct spatial zones: the back half (Z=0 to Z=13) will house a solid, enclosed convenience store, while the front half (Z=14 to Z=29) will be an open-air drive-through forecourt for the gas pumps. The structure is a mix of hollow interior space (the store) and tiered, floating architecture (the pump canopy).

I will use Stone as my primary utility material—it acts as the concrete foundation, the asphalt driveway, the structural pillars for the pumps, and the heavy roof of the canopy. I will use Dirt purely as a hidden foundation filler beneath the store to save on costly materials. I will construct the store's walls out of Bricks to give it a sturdy, classic commercial aesthetic. I will use Glass for the storefront so the cashier has a clear line of sight to the pumps. I will use Stone Slabs for interior shelving and flat roofing. I will use a Diamond Block at the front window—in this modded context, I will treat this as a high-tech cash register or a specialized pump-control console. Finally, I will use White Wool to line the edge of the gas canopy, providing a bright, clean, branded awning that catches the eye of passing drivers.

3. CONSTRUCTION SEQUENCE & LOGIC

Layer Y=0: The Foundation and Lot
I will begin by laying the groundwork. From Z=14 to Z=29, I will pave a massive, solid Stone driveway where vehicles will pull in. In the back half (Z=0 to Z=13), I will outline the convenience store's foundation with Stone and fill the interior floor area with Dirt. This establishes a clear boundary between the pedestrian retail space and the vehicular zone.

Layer Y=1: The Ground Floor and Pumps
I will now build the functional layer. I will erect the outer walls of the convenience store using Bricks. On the front wall facing the driveway, I will install Glass windows and place the Diamond Block right in the center to serve as the checkout console. Inside the store, I will place Stone and Stone Slabs to form the checkout counter and retail shelving. Out on the Stone driveway, I will place two distinct pairs of Stone blocks (at X=5,6 and X=10,11). These are the bases of my gas pumps.

Layer Y=2: Wall Extension
I will continue raising the vertical elements. I will extend the Brick walls of the store and the Glass windows of the storefront up by one block. Inside, I will continue stacking Stone Slabs to create multi-level shelves. Outside, I will add another layer of Stone to the gas pumps, bringing them to eye level for the customers.

Layer Y=3: Upper Walls and Pump Headers
I will cap off the functional height of the store and pumps. I will finish the Brick walls. Inside the store, I will arrange Stone blocks in a staggered pattern to represent tall display racks or overhead lighting fixtures. Out at the gas pumps, I will bridge the Stone pillars with Stone Slabs. This creates the digital display headers where the gas prices and gallons are shown.

Layer Y=4: Store Roof and Canopy Base
I will now focus on overhead protection. Over the convenience store, I will build a flat roof using a large sheet of Stone Slabs, bordered by a Brick trim. Out in the forecourt, I will begin constructing the massive gas canopy. I will suspend a large rectangle of Stone and Stone Slabs high above the pumps, creating a wide shadow that will protect drivers from the rain.

Layer Y=5: Parapets and Branded Awning
I will apply the final architectural polish. Around the flat roof of the convenience store, I will place a ring of Stone Slabs to act as a short parapet, preventing water runoff and hiding the roof seams. For the massive gas canopy in the front, I will wrap the entire outer edge in White Wool. This creates a striking, modern fascia board—a bright, branded rim that completes the iconic look of a highway gas station.

Architect's Plan:
As the Master Teacher, I will guide you through the spatial rationale for the "Plant Melon Watermelon" structure. This is a multi-tiered, vertical agricultural facility designed for growing melons and pumpkins (or watermelons). Let us break down the blueprint so you can visualize the architecture before placing a single block.

1. Footprint Analysis
I am looking at a structure that is 13 blocks wide (X-axis), 15 blocks deep (Z-axis), and 13 blocks tall (Y-axis). The footprint is solid at the very bottom, but as we move upward, it becomes a tiered, semi-hollow framework. The building is designed vertically to maximize crop yield within a small horizontal footprint, utilizing repeating modular layers.

2. Material Strategy
I will use a highly functional palette tailored for agriculture and mechanics:
- Grass (B) and Dirt (A): These form the foundation and the actual planting beds for the seeds and stems.
- Oak Logs (C): I will use these as vertical structural pillars at the corners and along the walls to give the build a sturdy, framed aesthetic.
- Stone Slabs (D): These are crucial. I will use them for walkways, flooring between tiers, and the roof. Slabs are economical and prevent hostile mobs from spawning.
- Chests (E): Positioned at the base, these will act as the collection hub for the harvested melons.
- Stone (F): This is our primary structural and mechanical block. In this blueprint, it represents the solid blocks supporting the crops, containing the water, and likely housing the automated harvesting mechanisms (like pistons and observers).
- Glass (G): I will place glass near the water and crops. This allows sunlight to reach the plants—essential for growth—while keeping the water safely contained.
- Water (H): Placed strategically on each farming tier to hydrate the dirt blocks.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic
I will build this structure from the ground up, dividing it into four logical phases: the foundation, the collection base, the farming tiers, and the roof.

Phase 1: The Foundation (Y=0)
At Y=0, I will lay down a solid 13x15 base. I will primarily use Grass blocks, but I will place a specific column of Dirt blocks along the left edge (X=0). This dirt acts as a marker and grounding point for the collection mechanisms that will sit above it.

Phase 2: The Collection Room (Y=1 to Y=3)
Moving up to Y=1 through Y=3, I am building the ground-level maintenance and storage area. I will place Oak Log pillars at the corners to establish the frame. On the left side (X=0 to X=2), I will place a series of Chests and Stone blocks. This is the central nervous system for item collection. I will surround the rest of the perimeter with Stone Slabs to create a clean, accessible walkway, leaving the center mostly hollow to accommodate the drop-chute for the falling melons.

Phase 3: The Vertical Farming Tiers (Y=4 to Y=10)
Here is where the core logic of the build shines. I will construct alternating layers of "Farming Beds" and "Mechanical Supports."
- The Farming Beds (Y=4, Y=6, Y=8, Y=10): At Y=4, I will step the footprint inward slightly. I will place a row of Dirt blocks in the center for planting. To the left and right of the dirt, I will place Water blocks to hydrate the soil. I will immediately cap the outer edges of the water with Glass to prevent spills while letting light in. Stone blocks will surround the dirt to provide a surface for the melons to grow onto. 
- The Mechanical Supports (Y=5, Y=7, Y=9): Directly above each farming bed, I will build a support layer using Stone and Stone Slabs. This layer serves a dual purpose: it acts as the ceiling for the crops below, and it provides the structural flooring for the next tier of dirt and water above. 

Phase 4: The Roof (Y=11 to Y=12)
Finally, I need to cap the structure to protect the crops. At Y=11, I will pull the walls inward using Stone Slabs and Stone, tapering the top of the building. At Y=12, I will lay down a completely solid, flat roof made entirely of Stone Slabs. I choose slabs here specifically so that no monsters can spawn on top of the farm at night.

By visualizing this alternating sequence—Foundation, Collection Base, alternating Farm/Support Tiers, and a Slab Roof—you can perfectly map out the 3D space of this automated agricultural tower.

The X-axis represents the long chassis and the stowed telescopic boom. The Z-axis represents the width of the vehicle, including its extended outriggers. I must choose materials that reflect the heavy industrial nature of this machine:
- Stone (B): This is my primary structural mass. I will use it for the heavy tires, the thick carrier chassis, the counterweights, and the massive telescopic boom.
- Stone Slab (A): I will use slabs for low-clearance areas under the chassis, flat walking decks, and thin roofs.
- Iron Block (C): I will use iron strategically for high-stress mechanical components, specifically the hydraulic outrigger jacks and the heavy boom-lift cylinders.
- Glass (D): I will use glass to create the two distinct cabins required for this vehicle: the lower driver's cab for road travel, and the upper operator's cab for crane work.
- Air (.): I will use air to carve out the wheel wells and separate the mechanical components.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic
I will build this crane from the ground up, layer by layer, ensuring every block serves a mechanical purpose.

Layer Y=0 (Wheels and Outrigger Pads):
I will start by laying down the 8 axles that give the "8.1" its name. Along Z=1 and Z=7, I will place 8 pairs of Stone blocks separated by air to represent the 16 massive tires. Down the center (Z=3 to 5), I will use Stone Slabs to create a low-hanging central chassis. On the extreme edges (Z=0 and Z=8), I will place isolated slabs to act as the deployed outrigger support pads.

Layer Y=1 (Main Carrier Chassis):
I will build the solid lower hull of the carrier deck. I will place solid Stone over the wheels to form the wheel arches and the heavy structural spine. Directly above the outrigger pads on the edges, I will place Iron Blocks; these represent the powerful hydraulic pistons that push the pads into the ground.

Layer Y=3 (Superstructure and Turntable):

I will lay the foundation for the massive telescopic boom, running horizontally down the center of the craft. At the pivot point near the front (X=36 to 39), I will place a cluster of Iron Blocks. These represent the heavy-duty hydraulic luffing cylinders required to raise the massive boom.

Layer Y=6 (Boom Top and Crane Operator's Cab):
I will cap the top of the boom with Stone. At the very rear of the superstructure (X=0 to X=2, offset to the side), I will place a new cluster of Glass blocks. This is the crane operator's cab. I must place it high and at the back so the operator has a clear, unobstructed view of the boom and the lifting area.

I will finish the build by placing Stone Slabs over the crane operator's cab to act as a roof. Finally, at the far front tip of the boom (X=32 to 39), I will place a few final Stone blocks to represent the heavy hook block and pulley system, stowed securely for transport.

Water is critical here; it serves a dual purpose of hydrating the sand and creating a flowing river to transport our harvested crops. I will use Chests for our collection system. For the structural and mechanical housing, I will use Cobblestone for retaining walls, Oak Planks for aesthetic framing, and smooth Stone as the mounting blocks for our redstone components (pistons and observers). Finally, I will place a few Furnaces at the top corners as utility stations for the farmer.

Construction Sequence:

At Y=0, I am laying the deep foundation. I will create a 30x5 footprint mostly out of Dirt. However, in the front row, I will leave a 15-block wide empty trench. Just behind this trench, I will place two sets of double Chests. These are the collection hubs where all our harvested sugarcane will eventually flow.

At Y=1, I am building up the earth around the collection area. I will continue placing Dirt, but I will leave air gaps directly above the chests to allow room for hoppers or item alignment. I will place a few Stone blocks near these gaps to act as structural markers for the drop zone.

At Y=2, I am establishing the surface level. I will ring the outer edges with Grass Blocks to make it look natural. Inside this ring, I will place strategic Water source blocks. These are hidden hydration pockets that will keep the soil wet and prepare the plumbing for the water streams above.

At Y=3, I am building the functional heart of the farm. Along the back-middle, I will lay down a massive 26-block long strip of Sand. This is our planting row. Directly in front of the sand, I will flood the area with Water. I will constrain this water using Cobblestone and Oak Plank retaining walls. This creates a horizontal flowing river that will catch falling sugarcane and sweep it directly into the collection chests below.

At Y=4, I am creating the harvesting mechanism layer. I must leave the space directly above the sand completely empty (Air) so the sugarcane has room to grow. Behind this empty space, I will build a solid line of Stone blocks. In a working farm, this stone ledge is where I will mount my pistons. When activated, the pistons will extend into the air space and snap the sugarcane stalks. I will frame the sides with Oak Planks to prevent the harvested items from flying out of bounds.

At Y=5, I am building the detection layer. Again, I will leave the growth chamber empty so the sugarcane can reach its maximum height. On the back wall, directly above the piston supports, I will place another row of Stone blocks. This is the observer ledge. These blocks will hold the sensors that watch the sugarcane; when the plant reaches this height, it will trigger the harvest.

At Y=6, I am capping the machine. I will cover the back half of the build with Cobblestone, Dirt, and Grass. This acts as a roof to conceal the redstone mechanics and creates a natural-looking walkway over the machine. At the far back corners, I will place a quirky combination of Furnaces, Sand, and Stone to serve as a small, functional workstation for the farmer.

At Y=7, I am installing the final redstone pathway. I will run a single, 29-block long line of Stone across the very top of the back wall. This acts as the conductive wire path, carrying the redstone signal from the observers down to the pistons, completing the loop of automation.

1. Footprint Analysis
I will define our canvas. The bounding box for this structure is 15 blocks wide (X-axis, 0 to 14), 19 blocks deep (Z-axis, 0 to 18), and 15 blocks tall (Y-axis, 0 to 14). 
This is a tiered, hollow structure. It features a narrow ground floor, a wider second story that overhangs the first—a hallmark of medieval architecture—and a steep, solid A-frame roof. The interior is hollow to allow for a living space.

2. Material Strategy
I will use a simple, rustic palette to achieve the medieval aesthetic:
- Grass (A) and Dirt (B): I will use these to anchor the house naturally into the terrain at Y=0.
- Oak Planks (C): I will use these for the interior floors. Wood provides a warm, habitable contrast to the cold exterior.
- Stone (D): This is our primary structural material. I will use it for the sturdy foundation, the walls, and the heavy, protective roof.
- Stone Slabs (E): I will use these for subtle detailing around the foundation and to create a smooth, capped ridge at the very peak of the roof.
- Glass (F): I will place these in the walls to serve as windows, breaking up the heavy stone and letting light into the hollow interior.
- Torches (G): I will place these strategically inside to illuminate the living spaces and the attic.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic
Now, I will walk you through the layers from the ground up. Visualize my steps.

Y=0 (The Ground & Foundation Floor): 
I will lay down a bed of grass and dirt to form the surrounding yard. In the center (roughly X=4 to X=9), I will embed a rectangular floor of Oak Planks. This is the ground floor of our interior.

Y=1 to Y=3 (First Floor Walls): 
I will build the ground floor walls using Stone. Notice that the footprint here is relatively tight, spanning from X=2 to X=10. I will leave a gap at the front for a doorway. At Y=2 and Y=3, I will insert Glass blocks into the Stone walls to create small, secure windows. I will also use Stone Slabs around the base to give the foundation a thicker, more grounded appearance.

Y=4 (The Overhang & Second Story Floor): 
Pay close attention here, Student. At Y=4, I am executing the classic medieval overhang. I will expand the footprint outward. The Stone outer ring now stretches from X=1 to X=11, hanging directly over the empty air outside the first-floor walls. Inside this wider Stone ring, I will fill the space with Oak Planks to create the floor for the second story. 

Y=5 to Y=7 (Second Floor Walls):

Y=8 (The Ceiling / Roof Base):

Y=9 to Y=13 (The A-Frame Roof): 
I will now construct a steep A-frame roof. To achieve this slope, I will step the Stone blocks inward on the X-axis with every single layer. 
- At Y=9, the roof spans X=1 to X=11.
- At Y=10, I will step it in to X=2 to X=10.
- I will continue this inward stepping (Y=11 is X=3 to X=9, Y=12 is X=4 to X=8, Y=13 is X=5 to X=7).

Y=14 (The Roof Peak):

I am looking at a long, linear defensive structure. The total dimensions are 5 blocks wide on the X-axis (though the outermost blocks are air, making the actual built width 3 blocks), 67 blocks long on the Z-axis, and 5 blocks high on the Y-axis. The structure is tiered, starting as three distinct segments on the ground that eventually merge into a single continuous bridge, topped with segmented battlements. The left side of the wall features hollow internal sections, while the right side is heavily solid.

2. Material Strategy
I will use a highly durable and visually striking palette to convey a fortified medieval aesthetic. 
- Stone (A): This is my primary structural anchor. I will use it to form the bulk of the walls, the arches over the gates, and the defensive battlements. It provides the necessary visual weight for a fortification.
- Oak Log (B): I will embed these vertically into the stone to act as structural pillars. This creates a classic timber-framed reinforcement pattern, breaking up the monotonous gray of the stone and adding a realistic architectural support system.
- Stone Slab (C): I will use these very sparingly near the top of the gate arches to create subtle depth, likely acting as minor indentations or footings for the guards.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic

Layer Y=0 (The Foundation):
I will establish the footprint by building three distinct ground-level structures. From Z=0 to 28, I will build the left wall segment. I will make the ends of this segment solid, but I will hollow out the center (Z=3 to 16) to create an internal corridor or save on materials. From Z=29 to 31, I will leave a 3-block wide air gap for the first gate entrance. At Z=32 to 34, I will build a solid 3x3 central pillar to divide the gate. I will leave another 3-block air gap from Z=35 to 37 for the second entrance. Finally, from Z=38 to 66, I will build the right wall segment, which I will make completely solid. Throughout this layer, I will alternate Stone and Oak Logs to set up my reinforced pillar pattern.

Layer Y=1 (Lower Wall & Slits):
I will continue building upward, maintaining the alternating Stone and Oak Log pattern. However, I will introduce strategic hollow points. I will hollow out the extreme ends of the walls and the center of the middle pillar. I should do this to create arrow slits or narrow windows for defenders on the ground to look through without exposing themselves to enemy fire.

Layer Y=2 (Upper Wall & Shifting Corridors):
I will build the final vertical layer of the supporting walls. I will make the right wall completely solid to maximize its defensive strength. On the left wall, I will shift the hollow internal corridor to a new section (Z=18 to 27). I will do this to create an internal staggered layout, perhaps representing a hidden staircase or a secondary defensive firing line. The central pillar remains solid to bear the weight of the upcoming arches.

Layer Y=3 (The Bridge and Walkway):
I will now connect the entire structure. I will lay down a nearly continuous line of solid Stone across the entire 67-block length. I will bridge the air gaps over the two gate entrances, effectively creating the flat roof of the gatehouse. I will place Stone Slabs at Z=26 and Z=40 to create slight textural dips in the floor. This layer serves as the main patrol walkway for my guards, allowing them to run from one end of the wall to the other without descending.

Layer Y=4 (The Battlements):
I will add the final defensive touches. I will not build a continuous wall here; instead, I will construct raised stone parapets in specific segments. I will build a 16-block long parapet on the left wall, a 5-block long parapet directly over the central gate, and another 16-block long parapet on the right wall. I will leave air gaps between these raised sections. I should do this to create classic crenellations, giving my archers heavy cover to hide behind while providing gaps to shoot down at anyone approaching the gate.

3. Torches: I will use Torches as 3D highlights. By attaching them to the front face of the wool, I am simulating the sparkling light reflections bouncing off the angled facets of the diamond.

Construction Sequence
I will build this structure from the ground up, layer by layer, keeping my main canvas locked to the X=2 axis.

At Y=0 and Y=1, I will construct the pedestal. I will place a single Stone block at Z=7 for both layers, creating a 2-block tall central pillar. This acts as the anchor for the heavy gem above.

At Y=2, I will begin the bottom tip of the diamond. I will place a 7-block wide row of White Wool centered directly over the pedestal (Z=4 to Z=10). 

At Y=3 and Y=4, I will angle the bottom edges of the diamond outward. I will expand the width to 9 blocks (Z=3 to Z=11), and then to 11 blocks (Z=2 to Z=12).

1. Footprint Analysis
I will be working within a bounding box that is 10 blocks wide (X-axis), 14 blocks deep (Z-axis), and 10 blocks tall (Y-axis). This structure is a two-story, hollow-interior building with a flat, tiered roof system. The footprint is slightly asymmetrical to accommodate an outdoor patio space.

2. Material Strategy
Modern architecture relies on clean lines, high contrast, and abundant natural light. 
- I will use Quartz Block (C) as my primary structural material; its smooth, bright white texture is the quintessential modern facade.
- I will use Glass (G) extensively for floor-to-ceiling windows to dissolve the boundary between indoors and outdoors.
- I will use Stone (F) for structural pillars and exterior accents to provide a stark, heavy contrast to the pristine quartz.
- I will use White Wool (D) for the interior floors and ceilings. This provides a soft, carpeted acoustic dampening inside, contrasting with the hard exterior.
- I will use Stone Slabs (E) to create a sleek, low-profile outdoor patio.
- I will use Grass (A) and Dirt (B) to integrate the foundation naturally into the surrounding landscape.

3. Construction Sequence & Logic
Let us walk through the layers from the ground up.

Layer Y=0 (Foundation and Landscaping):
I will establish the footprint. I will lay down a perimeter of grass and dirt to ground the build. Inside the footprint, I will outline the foundation with quartz and fill the interior floor with white wool to create a plush living room carpet. On the right side of the property (Z=8 to 11), I will lay down a stone slab patio to serve as an outdoor lounging area.

Layers Y=1 to Y=3 (First Floor Walls):
I will raise the first-floor walls, keeping the interior entirely hollow for the living space. I will build solid quartz walls where privacy is needed, but I will dedicate large sections of the facade to glass panels to create expansive modern windows. I will also erect vertical stone pillars on the outer edges of the footprint; these will frame the house and draw the eye upward.

Layer Y=4 (The Mid-Level Divider):
I will cap the first floor and create the foundation for the second. I will outline the perimeter with quartz to maintain the exterior white facade, but I will fill the entire interior of this layer with white wool. This serves a dual purpose: it acts as a clean, white ceiling for the first floor and a soft, carpeted floor for the second story.

Layers Y=5 to Y=7 (Second Floor Walls):
I will construct the second story, maintaining the hollow interior. I will continue the design language established below: quartz for the solid walls, expansive glass for the windows, and stone for the vertical structural pillars. The alignment of these materials with the first floor ensures a cohesive, geometric facade.

Layer Y=8 (The Flat Roof and Skylights):
I will seal the interior space. Because this is a modern design, I will build a perfectly flat roof. I will use quartz for the solid roofing, but I will strategically place large clusters of glass blocks in the center. These will act as massive skylights, flooding the second-floor interior with natural sunlight.

Layer Y=9 (Architectural Roof Beams):
I will add the final architectural flourish. Instead of leaving the roof completely flat and boring, I will lay down horizontal bands of stone spanning across the X-axis. These bands will alternate with empty air space, creating a slatted, pergola-style overhang above the flat roof. This provides shade, adds geometric complexity, and completes the modern aesthetic.

Architect's Plan:
Footprint Analysis: I am building a Dropper item elevator. I need to plan a 3D grid that is 6 blocks wide on the X axis, 9 blocks tall on the Y axis, and 6 blocks deep on the Z axis. This structure is not a solid building, but rather a skeletal, vertical redstone contraption. The base is wide and flat to accommodate input chests and a redstone clock, while the middle section narrows into a tight 1 by 2 vertical column for the elevator shaft, finally branching out slightly at the top for the output collection.

Material Strategy: I will use Droppers as the core of this build because they can shoot items upwards into each other. I will use Hoppers and Chests to create a massive input buffer and a secure output destination. For the logic, I will use a Comparator to detect when items enter the system, which will trigger a Sticky Piston, Repeater, and Observer clock. To carry the redstone signal all the way up the shaft, I will use an alternating tower of Observers and Redstone Wire. I will also use a Birch Sign at the base, which serves as a non-solid spacer block to prevent redstone cross-wiring while keeping the footprint compact.

Construction Sequence: 
At Y=0, I will build the engine and the input funnels. I will place the foundational upward-facing dropper at X=2, Z=2. To feed items into this dropper, I will attach two horizontal lines of hoppers: one extending east to X=5, and another extending south to Z=5. To make the elevator fire automatically, I will build a detection circuit. I will place a comparator at X=2, Z=1 to read the dropper. This will power a repeater and a sticky piston at X=0, which will push an observer to create a rapid ticking clock whenever items are present.

At Y=1, I will begin the vertical ascent and add bulk storage. I will place the second dropper directly above the first. Next to it at X=1, Z=2, I will place an observer to catch the redstone pulses from the clock below. To handle massive amounts of items, I will place chests on top of the outer hoppers from the previous layer, creating large input buffers.

From Y=2 to Y=7, I will construct the main elevator shaft. I will stack droppers facing upwards at X=2, Z=2 all the way to the top. To ensure every dropper fires, I will build a power tower directly adjacent to them at X=1, Z=2. I will alternate my materials here. I will place redstone wire on the even layers like Y=2, Y=4, and Y=6, and I will place observers on the odd layers like Y=3, Y=5, and Y=7. This alternating pattern guarantees that the rapid pulse from the base travels instantly up the tower, powering every dropper simultaneously without locking them.

At Y=8, I will build the output terminal. I will place the final dropper at X=2, Z=2 and the final piece of redstone wire next to it. Instead of shooting items into the sky, I will place a hopper at X=2, Z=1 that catches the items from the top dropper. Finally, I will place an output chest at X=2, Z=0. The items will flow from the top dropper, through the hopper, and safely into this chest, completing the elevator system.

Architect's Plan:
As the Master Teacher, I will guide you through the spatial visualization of our new project: the 'Rhinocéros'. Before we look at the raw coordinates, I want you to build this magnificent beast in your mind's eye. 

Footprint Analysis:
I will be working within a bounding box that is 12 blocks long (X=1 to X=12), 6 blocks high (Y=0 to Y=5), and 5 blocks wide (Z=1 to Z=5). This is not a hollow architectural building; it is a solid, sculpted organic structure. The X-axis represents the length of the animal, with X=1 being the tip of the nose/horn and X=12 being the tail. The Z-axis represents the width, with Z=3 acting as the exact center line of the spine, and Z=1 and Z=5 acting as the outer flanks.

Material Strategy:
I will use a very restricted palette to emphasize form over color. 
First, I will use Stone (A) for 99% of the build. I choose Stone because its gray, monolithic texture perfectly mimics the thick, heavy, leathery hide of a rhinoceros. It gives the beast a sense of immense weight and durability.
Second, I will use Stone Slabs (B) very sparingly. I will place these half-blocks only at the lower jaw. I do this to create a subtle upward slope for the underbelly of the head, preventing the snout from looking like a blunt, square box.

Construction Sequence:
Let's build this layer by layer, from the ground up.

Layer Y=0 (The Hooves):
I will start by planting the four massive legs on the ground. I will not build a solid floor. Instead, I will create four distinct 2x2 pillars. The front legs will be positioned at X=5 and X=6. The back legs will be placed further back at X=10 and X=11. I will place these legs on the outer edges (Z=1,2 and Z=4,5), leaving the center line (Z=3) completely empty so the air flows under the beast's belly.

Layer Y=1 (Upper Legs and Lower Jaw):
I will continue building the legs upward, but I will start fleshing out the body. I will extend the back legs forward to X=9 to create thick, muscular thighs. At the center line (Z=3), I will bridge the gap between the front and back legs to form the lowest part of the belly. At the very front (X=2 and X=3, Z=3), I will place my Stone Slabs. This forms the sloping lower jaw of the rhino, jutting out ahead of the front legs.

Layer Y=2 (The Lower Torso and Snout):
I will now build the main bulk of the lower body. I will fill in a massive, solid core from X=2 all the way to X=11. The flanks will bulge outward to Z=1 and Z=5, giving the rhino its characteristic heavy girth. At the very front center (X=1, Z=3), I will place a single stone block. This is the foundational base of the rhino's iconic front horn, extending past the jaw.

Layer Y=3 (The Core and Tail):
I will construct the thickest, most solid part of the torso. This layer is a dense block of muscle. At the back center (X=12, Z=3), I will place a single block extending past the hindquarters to represent a small tail. At the front, I will continue building the horn upward at X=1. I will also add blocks on the outer edges of the head (X=3, Z=1 and Z=5) to form the thick cheeks.

Layer Y=4 (The Shoulders and Spine):
I will begin tapering the body inward to form the arched back. I will create pronounced, muscular shoulder humps at X=6 and hip bumps at X=9 and X=10 on the outer edges. I will continue the central spine down the middle (Z=3). At the front, I will extend the horn up yet another block at X=1, Z=3, showing just how massive this weapon is.

Layer Y=5 (The Crest, Ears, and Horn Tip):
I will finish the sculpture by adding the defining upper details. I will place the sharp, final tip of the main horn at the very front (X=1, Z=3). Moving slightly back, I will build the crown of the head and place two distinct ears sticking out at X=4, Z=1 and Z=5.
